ladder.name: Novice
ladder.can: Open a CSV in a spreadsheet and work out totals, averages, biggest and smallest values and counts on a range: SUM, AVERAGE, MIN, MAX, COUNTA, ROUND.
ladder.proof: Timed Rank Trial on the page: 6 problems, 5 to pass, no hints.
ladder.benchmark: Can answer simple 'how much in total' questions from a sheet.

ladder.name: Beginner
ladder.can: Count and add with conditions (COUNTIF, COUNTIFS, SUMIF, SUMIFS), label rows with IF and AND, and clean messy text before counting it.
ladder.proof: Timed Rank Trial on the page: 6 problems, 5 to pass, no hints.
ladder.benchmark: Where a typical intro spreadsheet course leaves you.

ladder.name: Competent
ladder.can: Combine formulas to summarise a sheet you haven't seen: several conditions at once, averages for a subset, shares as percentages and a summary grid with $ references.
ladder.proof: Timed Rank Trial on the page, at least half on data or scenarios you haven't practised: 6 problems, 5 to pass, no hints.
ladder.benchmark: Builds a reliable summary from a new export without help.

ladder.name: Proficient
ladder.can: Lookups (XLOOKUP, or INDEX with MATCH), pivot tables, data validation and tidy multi-tab workbooks, on unfamiliar data.
ladder.proof: Timed Rank Trial on the page, at least half on data or scenarios you haven't practised: 6 problems, 5 to pass, no hints.
ladder.benchmark: The person the team asks to fix a broken workbook.

ladder.name: Advanced
ladder.can: Dynamic array formulas (FILTER, UNIQUE, SORT), LET and LAMBDA, and repeatable data cleaning with Power Query or a similar tool.
ladder.proof: Rank Trial on hard problems, plus outside evidence.
ladder.benchmark: Builds workbooks others run every week without breaking.
ladder.evidence: A real certification at an expert level for your spreadsheet tool, or a public workbook using dynamic arrays and repeatable cleaning, reviewed by an experienced user.

ladder.name: Expert
ladder.can: Designs workbook models others rely on, audits formulas for errors, and keeps large workbooks fast and readable.
ladder.proof: Rank Trial plus outside evidence, reviewed by an experienced modeller.
ladder.benchmark: Trusted to build and review models for a whole department.
ladder.evidence: A public model on open data with documentation and an error audit, reviewed and signed off by an experienced modeller.

ladder.name: Master
ladder.can: Top-level spreadsheet knowledge: calculation engine behaviour, advanced modelling standards, and teaching and reviewing others' workbooks.
ladder.proof: Outside evidence of standing, plus peer review. No page trial can prove this level.
ladder.benchmark: Recognised beyond your own team as a spreadsheet authority.
ladder.evidence: Public teaching or answers others rely on, plus a written review of your work by a recognised expert.

problems.goal: In `team-expenses.csv` as downloaded, January is rows 2-21. What's the **total** of the January claims?
February is rows 22-41. What's the **average** February claim, rounded to 2 decimal places?
March is rows 42-61. What's the **biggest** March claim?
What's the **smallest** January claim (rows 2-21)?
What's the **total** of February and March together (rows 22-61)?
How far apart are the biggest and smallest claims in the whole sheet? Type the difference.
What's the average **January** claim (rows 2-21), rounded to the **nearest whole pound**?

problems.q: A sheet has prices in C2 to C40 and a total row at C41. Which formula gives the average price without the total row?
options: =AVERAGE(C1:C41)
=AVERAGE(C2:C40)
=AVERAGE(C2:C41)
problems.why: Stop the range above the total row. Dividing by 41 counts a row that isn't a price.

problems.q: You need the number of rows in a list of names in B2 to B90. Which formula counts them?
options: =SUM(B2:B90)
=MAX(B2:B90)
=COUNTA(B1:B1)
=COUNTA(B2:B90)
problems.why: COUNTA counts filled cells, including text. SUM and MAX only work on numbers.

problems.q: A report needs money to the penny, and a later formula uses the value. What should you use?
options: ROUND(value, 2) in the formula itself
The decrease-decimal button twice
Format the cell as currency only
Type the rounded number over it
problems.why: ROUND changes the value. Display formats only change how it looks.

problems.goal: How many claims did **Ben** make?
How much was claimed for **Meals** in total?
How much was claimed for **Software** in total? Careful: this is the file as downloaded.
How many claims are **over 100 pounds**?
How much does **Femi** have in **Pending** claims?
How many **Travel** claims have **no receipt**?
Label claims of **200 pounds or more** as Big. How many Big claims are there?

problems.q: A manager wants the total cost on rows where region is North and status is Open. Which formula fits?
options: SUMIF with both tests inside one set of quotes
SUMIFS with the cost range first, then two test pairs
COUNTIFS with the two tests, then add the cost
SUM of the cost column with a filter left on
problems.why: SUMIFS takes several tests and adds the matching costs. COUNTIFS counts rows, it doesn't add money.

problems.q: Your COUNTIF for "Closed" misses some rows that clearly say Closed. What's the likely cause?
options: COUNTIF only counts upper-case text
COUNTIF can't count more than 50 rows
The rows are sorted in the wrong order
Some cells hold a hidden space or a typo
problems.why: Spaces and typos make different values. COUNTIF ignores case and sort order.

problems.q: You want a column saying Late when days is over 5 and paid is No. Which formula is right for row 2?
options: =IF(AND(C2>5, D2="No"), "Late", "OK")
=IF(C2>5, D2="No", "Late", "OK")
=IF(OR(C2>5, D2="No"), "Late", "OK")
=AND(IF(C2>5), D2="No", "Late")
problems.why: Both tests must be true, so AND goes inside IF. OR would label rows that pass only one test.

problems.goal: `trip-expenses.csv` lists the costs of three team trips. What did the **Glasgow** trip cost in total?
In `trip-expenses.csv`, what's the average **Hotel** cost, rounded to 2 decimal places?
In `trip-expenses.csv`, who spent the most on **Taxi** across all trips? Type the name.
In `trip-expenses.csv`, what percentage of bookings were **booked early**? Round to a whole number.
In `trip-expenses.csv`, how much did **Train** tickets for **Leeds** cost when they were **not** booked early?
Back on `team-expenses.csv` (Software fixed): what's the average **Approved** claim, rounded to 2 decimal places?
In `team-expenses.csv`, which month had the most money claimed? Type Jan, Feb or Mar.

problems.q: You fill =SUMIFS(D2:D50, B2:B50, $A2, C2:C50, B$1) down and across a grid, and the totals drift wrong lower down. What's missing?
options: A $ on the A in $A2, which already has one there
$ signs on the data ranges, so they stop moving
A ROUND around the SUMIFS to tidy the decimals
An extra test pair for the row labels in column A
problems.why: Without $ the data ranges slide down as you fill, and miss rows. Lock them with $D$2:$D$50 and so on.

problems.q: A team lead wants the average order value for the North region only. Which formula works with SUMIF and COUNTIF?
options: SUMIF of North orders divided by COUNTA of all rows
COUNTIF of North divided by SUMIF of North orders
SUM of all orders divided by COUNTIF of North rows
SUMIF of North orders divided by COUNTIF of North
problems.why: An average for a subset is that subset's total over that subset's count. Dividing by all rows gives a share, not an average.

problems.q: A summary grid's grand total doesn't match the plain SUM of the data. What do you check first?
options: Labels in the grid that don't match the data's spelling
Whether the grid is on a tab to the left of the data
The number of decimal places shown in each cell
Whether the data tab has its filter turned on
problems.why: A label that doesn't match makes zeros, so money goes missing. Tab order and display don't change values.
